overview: This file traces the regulation and proposed expansion of civil and international aviation in occupied Japan from August 1947 through March 1949. It begins with an internal U.S. proposal to permit commercial airlines to carry passengers, mail, and cargo, then documents repeated Soviet violations of SCAP air-traffic rules at Haneda and the resulting enforcement measures. A substantial section contains SCAP Circular No. 14, with detailed routes, communications procedures, emergency rules, maps, and navigational aids. Later papers concern Pan American World Airways’ proposal to operate an internal U.S.-flag airline in Japan, the slow progress of Far Eastern Commission policy, and subsequent revisions of international air-traffic regulations.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on reopening commercial aviation in Japan
subfiles.from: Mr. Whitman, State Department Japan-Korea office
subfiles.about: The memorandum recommends allowing commercial airlines to transport cargo and mail as well as authorized passengers to and from Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reopening of limited private trade on August 15 made commercial air service urgent even though the Far Eastern Commission had not completed a civil-aviation policy. The memorandum argues that SCAP’s administrative discretion should encompass passengers, cargo, and mail and proposes notifying Pan American and Northwest accordingly.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1350 on Soviet air-traffic violations
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards a SCAP memorandum protesting dangerous violations of Japanese air-traffic regulations by Soviet aircraft.
subfiles.summary: Soviet aircraft cleared for flights to and from the Soviet Union repeatedly violated procedures while approaching Haneda. The Acting Political Adviser reports that the violations endangered other traffic and that further offending commanders could be denied entry into Japan.

subfiles.title: SCAP memorandum on control of Soviet international aircraft
subfiles.from: SCAP General Headquarters, signed by R. M. Levy for the Supreme Commander
subfiles.to: Soviet Member, Allied Council for Japan
subfiles.about: The surviving portion of the memorandum specifies Soviet violations and demands compliance with SCAP Circular No. 11.
subfiles.summary: The fragment records that the crew of Catalina No. 29 heard Haneda’s calls but refused to answer because controllers did not use the Soviet code word. It lists failures involving approach patterns, English-language communications, Tokyo Control, Ground Controlled Approach, and minimum altitude. Future offenders were to be grounded, investigated, and potentially denied entry.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1386 on further Soviet violations
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, Acting Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Sebald reports additional Soviet infringements and the temporary grounding of two aircraft at Haneda.
subfiles.summary: A Soviet request for November flights omitted the required designation of English-speaking crew members. Two Soviet aircraft arriving on November 4 were grounded after landing without contacting Haneda control, and no November clearances were to be issued until Soviet crews complied with SCAP regulations.

subfiles.title: Kislenko letter requesting November flight clearances
subfiles.from: Major General Kislenko, Acting Soviet Member, Allied Council for Japan
subfiles.to: Major General Mueller, Chief of Staff, SCAP
subfiles.about: Kislenko requests clearance for two Soviet Catalina aircraft to fly from Vladivostok to Tokyo with food and mail.
subfiles.summary: The request covers flights on November 3, 10, 17, and 24, 1947, and supplies complete crew rosters for Catalinas Nos. 24 and 29. Although related cover papers cite October 23, the reproduced letter itself bears October 25.

subfiles.title: SCAP reply on Soviet November aircraft clearances
subfiles.from: SCAP General Headquarters, signed by R. M. Levy
subfiles.to: Soviet Member, Allied Council for Japan
subfiles.about: SCAP makes approval of the requested Soviet flights conditional on compliance with English-language and communications requirements.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum invokes Circular No. 11 and the earlier October 16 warning. It requires each aircraft to designate an English-speaking crew member and each crew to be briefed on communications with Tokyo Control and Haneda Tower before clearance will be considered.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1456 forwarding revised air-traffic regulations
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards SCAP Circular No. 14, which replaced the previous rules for international air traffic in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Circular No. 14 superseded Circular No. 11 and established revised standard procedures for aircraft entering or leaving Japan. The despatch relates the new circular to the broader entry-and-exit rules contained in SCAP Circular No. 8.

subfiles.title: SCAP Circular No. 14: International Air Traffic in Japan
subfiles.from: SCAP General Headquarters; by command of General MacArthur
subfiles.to: Countries, agencies, and aircrews operating international flights into Japan
subfiles.about: The circular establishes detailed routes, arrival and departure rules, communications procedures, and emergency requirements for international aircraft.
subfiles.summary: Aircraft were directed through specified checkpoints and airways to Haneda, with escort instructions and restrictions on overflying airfields. The rules required English-language radio capability, use of the call word “New Comer,” contact with Tokyo Control and Haneda Tower, and compliance with Ground Controlled Approach procedures. They also addressed emergencies, rescue services, minimum altitude, weapons, and detention of improperly cleared aircraft.

subfiles.title: Circular No. 14 Inclosure 1: Standard Light Signals
subfiles.from: SCAP General Headquarters
subfiles.about: The enclosure defines portable traffic-control light signals for aircraft in flight and on the airfield.
subfiles.summary: Green, red, flashing red, and alternating red-and-green signals conveyed landing, circling, stopping, taxiing, takeoff, recall, and warning instructions. The system was intended to control aircraft without usable radio communications as well as personnel and vehicles on the landing area.

subfiles.title: Circular No. 14 Inclosure 2: Air Routes into Tokyo Area
subfiles.from: SCAP General Headquarters
subfiles.about: The enclosure is a map of prescribed air routes into the Tokyo area.
subfiles.summary: The page contains the mapped counterpart to the routes described in Circular No. 14. Its purpose was to guide cleared international flights toward the Tokyo and Haneda control area.

subfiles.title: Circular No. 14 Inclosure 3: Tokyo Area
subfiles.from: SCAP General Headquarters
subfiles.about: The map identifies checkpoints and major terrain features used by aircraft approaching Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: It marks Sado Island, Ryōtsu, Niigata, Nagaoka, Kōriyama, Maebashi, Koga, Tokyo, Yokohama, Izu Ōshima, and Mount Fuji. These locations correspond to the northern and southern approach routes prescribed in the circular.

subfiles.title: Circular No. 14 Inclosure 4: Radio Navigational Aids
subfiles.from: SCAP General Headquarters
subfiles.about: The enclosure charts radio navigational aids serving Haneda, Tokyo, and Izu Ōshima.
subfiles.summary: It lists the Haneda homer, Tokyo range, and Izu Ōshima range with coordinates, frequencies, and identification signals. The text identifies Haneda Airfield Operations as the source for current changes in radio facilities and flight data; “Manoda” is an evident OCR error for Haneda.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 654 on Soviet IL-12 violations
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch reports air-traffic violations committed by Soviet IL-12 No. 2 on September 22, 1948.
subfiles.summary: The aircraft failed to contact Tokyo Control and its escort, disregarded parking instructions, and arrived with only three and one-half hours’ notice instead of twenty-four. It was detained at Haneda pending investigation and released after a formal SCAP memorandum was delivered to the Soviet member of the Allied Council.

subfiles.title: Saltzman letter commenting on Eberle’s proposed reply
subfiles.from: Charles E. Saltzman
subfiles.about: Saltzman recommends removing a specific sixty-day prediction from Eberle’s reply concerning Japanese civil-aviation policy.
subfiles.summary: Saltzman warns that agreement on policy may not be achieved within sixty days. He proposes telling Pan American to withhold further action until the policy develops and receives final approval; drafting initials date the text November 24, while the page bears a November 29 office stamp.

subfiles.title: Routing slip assigning the Eberle correspondence to Auchincloss
subfiles.from: C. E. Conger
subfiles.about: The slip assigns action on the Eberle correspondence to Auchincloss and sends the original to Mr. Hllich for information.
subfiles.summary: Auchincloss was given an action assignment under control number 4027 with a November 17 suspense date. The original was separately routed for information.

subfiles.title: Information-copy routing slip
subfiles.from: C. E. Conger
subfiles.to: Unidentified recipient; carbon copy to J. W. Auchincloss
subfiles.about: The slip routes an information copy while directing a carbon copy to Auchincloss for action.
subfiles.summary: The principal recipient is illegible in the OCR. The remarks make clear that Auchincloss was responsible for action under control number 4027.

subfiles.title: Eberle letter requesting State Department views
subfiles.from: Brigadier General G. L. Eberle
subfiles.about: Eberle asks the State Department to review a proposed response to Pan American’s plan for an internal airline in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Eberle explains that Pan American had been advised to submit its proposal to SCAP, but SCAP declined to take the initiative while a policy paper remained before the Far Eastern Commission. He outlines FEC 245/20, including a proposed sixty-day mechanism, and raises the possibility of an interim U.S. directive or use of SCAP’s administrative authority.

subfiles.title: Bixby letter proposing a U.S.-flag airline within Japan
subfiles.from: H. M. Bixby, Pan American World Airways System
subfiles.about: Bixby seeks guidance on formally presenting Pan American’s proposal to establish and operate an internal commercial airline in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Bixby recounts an August meeting and Mr. Bond’s subsequent personal presentation of the proposal to General MacArthur in Tokyo. MacArthur expressed interest but believed Washington should take the initiative, and Pan American did not wish to press its plan if doing so would cause embarrassment.

subfiles.title: Draft reply to H. M. Bixby
subfiles.from: G. L. Eberle, draft
subfiles.about: The draft advises Pan American to delay further action while Washington considers Japanese civil-aviation policy.
subfiles.summary: It acknowledges MacArthur’s view that the initiative should come from Washington. The original draft predicts agreement within sixty days and asks Pan American to wait approximately that long before reopening discussions.

subfiles.title: Amrine memorandum on the Pan American proposal
subfiles.from: H. F. Amrine
subfiles.about: Amrine recommends softening Eberle’s proposed timetable for resolving Japanese civil-aviation policy.
subfiles.summary: After consulting Allison and Barnett, Amrine concludes that the sixty-day estimate is unduly optimistic because there is no assurance of prompt Far Eastern Commission action. He supplies replacement language advising Pan American to wait until the policy has developed and received final action.

subfiles.title: Auchincloss memorandum transmitting proposed answer
subfiles.from: J. W. Auchincloss
subfiles.about: Auchincloss submits the proposed reply to Eberle for review and signature processing.
subfiles.summary: Auchincloss states that he incorporated Amrine’s suggested modification of Eberle’s draft. Because Claxton knew more about the relevant Far Eastern Commission paper, he was asked to approve and forward the reply for signature.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 762 forwarding SCAP Circular No. 30
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards a revised SCAP circular governing international air traffic in Japan.
subfiles.summary: SCAP Circular No. 30, dated November 16, 1948, updated the earlier international air-traffic provisions. Copies were also designated for U.S. military authorities in Germany and for Seoul, but the circular itself is not present in the OCR bundle.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 158 forwarding SCAP Circular No. 6
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards a SCAP circular making minor changes to international air-traffic regulations.
subfiles.summary: SCAP Circular No. 6, dated March 9, 1949, amended the preceding rules governing international aviation in Japan. The reference to Despatch No. 762 as dated December 6, 1949 is an evident error for December 6, 1948; the enclosed circular is not reproduced in the OCR text.

interest: The bundle is especially useful for showing how occupation authorities combined diplomatic pressure, technical regulation, and physical detention of aircraft to enforce control over Japan’s airspace. The Soviet cases provide unusually concrete evidence about cockpit communications, language requirements, landing procedures, and recurring Allied-Soviet friction at Haneda. The Pan American correspondence also exposes the gap between corporate ambitions and the slow policy machinery of the Far Eastern Commission, while Circular No. 14 preserves a detailed snapshot of routes, radio frequencies, signals, and emergency infrastructure in early postwar Japanese aviation.
